9           Q.      How do data centers use energy?

10          A.      Data centers use some amount of energy for data processing. That usage

11   is not expected to be weather-sensitive. Data centers use energy for maintaining

12   habitable workspaces and temperature-controlled storage spaces, if necessary. That

13   usage is expected to be exactly as weather sensitive as any other commercial workspace

14   and temperature-controlled warehouse, respectively. Data centers also use energy for

15   process cooling, this usage is both process sensitive (meaning little energy is consumed

16   if the data center is not actively processing or accessing data), and weather sensitive in

17   most cases.

18          Q.      What systems can be used for process cooling?

19          A.      At a high level, data processors can be air cooled or water cooled.

20   Air cooling is conceptually like the little fan the blows in a desktop computer. Water

21   cooling is conceptually like the water jacket on the engine in your car, in which coolant is

22   circulated around the hot parts, and that heat is absorbed into the coolant.


                                               Page 7
      Conforming Direct Testimony of
     Sarah L.K. Lange

1           Q.     What is a “closed loop,” as that term is used in discussions of data

2    centers?

3           A.     Again, think of the cooling system in a conventional automobile. Coolant

4    in the water jacket is absorbs heat from the operating engine, then travels into the

5    radiator. The coolant rejects heat to the atmosphere through the fins of the radiator, and

6    then is pushed by the water pump back into the water jacket. Under normal operating

7    conditions, the same coolant is used over and over for many many cycles of heat

8    absorption and rejection. The coolant travels in a closed loop. In contrast, a boat motor

9    pulls water from the lake or river into its water jacket, the coolant absorbs heat from the

10   engine, and then the heated coolant is discharged back into the lake or the river. The

11   cooling system for a boat motor of this design is not a closed loop.

12          Q.     In a closed loop system, how is the heat rejected from the coolant? What

13   performs the job of a car radiator in the data center context?

14          A.     In a data center closed-loop, an industrial evaporative chiller or an

15   industrial compressor can be used to reject absorbed heat from the process that has

16   been absorbed into the closed loop system into the atmosphere.

17          Q.     What is an industrial compressor like?

18          A.     An industrial compressor is like an air conditioner or a refrigerator. Heat is

19   absorbed from the primary closed loop of coolant (coming from the processors) into a

20   secondary loop of refrigerant. The primary closed loop rejects heat into the refrigerant

21   loop. An electric motor compresses the refrigerant, and that extracts heat from the

22   refrigerant into the atmosphere.


                                               Page 8
      Conforming Direct Testimony of
     Sarah L.K. Lange

1           Q.     What is an evaporative chiller like?

2           A.     An evaporative chiller is like a person who is sweating.

3           Q.     How does an evaporative chiller work?

4           A.     An evaporative chiller works by placing water into contact with the thing to

5    be cooled (in the case of a data center, the primary closed loop, in the case of a human,

6    your skin) and as the water evaporates the residual water drops in temperature.

7           Q.     Can the water placed into contact with the thing to be cooled be reused?

8           A.     In part yes, and in part, no. If the water that is deposited onto the primary

9    cold loop is colder than the fluid inside the primary closed loop, some heat will reject

10   from the primary closed loop into the secondary loop of water. However, eventually, the

11   secondary loop of water would obtain temperature parity with the coolant in the primary

12   loop, or the secondary loop of water would be warmed by atmospheric conditions until

13   parity with the primary loop is reached, or some combination of those two factors

14   otherwise removes the ability of the primary loop to reject heat into the secondary loop.

15   In practice, an evaporative chiller works at least in part through the evaporation of water

16   into the atmosphere, dropping the temperature of the remailing secondary fluid. This

17   effectiveness of this process is dependent on the wet bulb temperature.

18          Q.     An industrial chiller uses electric energy like an air conditioner would. How

19   does an evaporative chiller use electric energy?

20          A.     An evaporative chiller must use electric energy to pump the coolant around

21   the primary closed loop, and will generally require energy to pump the secondary loop up,

22   over, and down the heat exchanger between the primary and secondary loops.

2           Q.      In general, what is the true-up plug and why is it used?

3           A.      A true-up plug is a temporary adjustment to the revenue requirement

4    calculation to essentially estimate conditions that will be in place as of the true-up cut

5    off. A familiar example would be when a new power plant is being built, with an in-service

6    date between the end of the update period and the true-up cut off. In that example, if

8    include a true-up plug to allow for meaningful local public hearings, useful class cost

9    of service and rate design work, and to generally apprise the Commission of Staff’s

10   expectation of the overall increase that will be in rates taking effect at the end of the case.

2           The Annualization Process
3           Q.     Can you explain what annualization means?

4           A.     Yes. Annualization refers to an adjustment that is made to reflect known

5    conditions at the end of the test period. For example, if mailing a bill costs $0.50 cents

6    per bill for 100 bills each month, the mailing expense is $50 per month. If at the end of

7    the test period, mailing expense increases to $0.75 per bill, then the earlier months would
